title: Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, Picasso
subject: art
description: Five nudes built from facets and masks: Les Demoiselles d'Avignon breaks with imitation and opens the door to Cubism. Even Picasso's friends were scandalized.

hero.hook: The painting Picasso kept turned to the wall, right before it changed art.

blocks.text: In **1907**, in Montmartre, **Picasso** finished *Les Demoiselles d'Avignon*. Five women, broken bodies, faces turned into masks. The seed of [[Cubism]] is already there.
Even his closest friends were shocked. Gone was [[mimesis]], the gentle imitation of the real.

Picasso worked at [[Le Bateau-Lavoir (Montmartre)]], a run-down block full of penniless artists. The title points to a street in Barcelona known for its brothels. The nude is no longer a Greek ideal: it is frontal and unsettling.
Dozens of studies came before the canvas. Picasso hesitated, corrected, hardened his lines. The result is not improvisation: it is a calculated attack on good taste.

blocks.caption: Five stares that no longer flatter

blocks.text: The faces on the right draw on African and Iberian [[arts premiers]]. This is [[Primitivism in modern art]]: looking for a force outside the European academic canon.
The two figures on the right, the most mask-like of all, mark the break. We move from the Western nude to another logic of the face, more conceptual than fleshly.
Picasso held the painting back for years, well aware of how violent it was.
The faceted planes announce [[analytical cubism]]. Braque, stunned at first, soon joined Picasso in taking space apart.
Rarely shown for years, the canvas still shaped Braque and everything cubist that followed. Its violence needed time to become “classic.”

blocks.caption: From ritual mask to modern grid

blocks.text: Now at MoMA, the painting is still the “big bang” of 20th-century art. Everything that breaks the visible into pieces owes it something.
To really grasp Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, keep one thing in mind: every technical detail serves an emotion or an idea. The work is never merely decorative.
Context counts as much as style. Dates, places, patrons, audience: all of it explains why a form appears at one precise moment, and not before.
Finally, a legacy is measured over the long run. What we see today in museums, films, or popular music still carries the mark of these inventions.
At MoMA it is now a required stop. It is easy to forget that it first scandalized even the avant-garde.
To really grasp Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, keep one thing in mind: every technical detail serves an emotion or an idea. The work is never merely decorative.
In 1907, Les Demoiselles d'Avignon shattered the classical nude and opened the road to Cubism.
